body:
Search “should I become a real estate agent” and most of what comes back is either a sales pitch from a real estate school or a discouraging thread on Reddit. Neither is a straight answer. The honest answer is that real estate is a good career for a specific kind of person, and a bad one for everyone else. Here is what that actually means, without the hype.

You are self-employed. Read that twice.

A real estate agent is not an employee of a brokerage. You are an independent contractor who hangs your license under a broker. That means no base salary, no guaranteed hours, and no paycheck the first, second, or sometimes third week you’re on the job. Every dollar you earn comes from a closed transaction. If that sentence makes you uneasy, sit with it before you enroll in a pre-license course, because it does not get easier once you’re licensed. It’s the fundamental shape of the job.

The upside of that same fact is real: no ceiling on what you can earn, no one telling you when you can take a Tuesday off, and full ownership of the business you build. But it is a trade, not a bonus. You are trading stability for upside. Be honest with yourself about which one you need more right now.

What the job actually is, day to day

New agents often picture the job as showing beautiful homes and handing over keys. Most of the actual job is less cinematic: answering calls at inconvenient hours, following up with leads who go quiet, driving to inspections and appraisals, filling out disclosure paperwork correctly, and prospecting for the next client before the current deal has even closed. It is sales and operations work wearing a real estate label. If you like people, don’t mind rejection, and can manage your own schedule without a manager standing over you, that combination suits the job. If you need structure imposed on you from outside, the freedom of the role can become a trap instead of a benefit.

The income reality, honestly

There is no single number for what an agent makes, and anyone who gives you one confidently is guessing or selling something. Income depends entirely on transactions closed, and transactions depend on your pipeline, your training, and how long you’ve been building relationships in your market. What is true across almost every market is that income is back-loaded: it is slow to start and compounds later as referrals and repeat clients take over from cold prospecting.

Rather than estimate a number here, run your own. Adams, Cameron & Co.’s real estate agent income estimator walks through realistic transaction volume and commission splits so you can see a range grounded in your own assumptions, not a marketing number.

The first year is the hard part

Almost every honest conversation with a working agent about their first year sounds the same: it was slower and harder than they expected, and the agents who made it through had two things in common. First, they had enough savings or another income source to cover several months of lean cash flow while the pipeline built. Second, they had a brokerage that gave them real training and leads instead of a desk and a login. Talent and likability matter, but a support system that gets you in front of clients while you’re still learning the ropes is what actually determines whether you make it to year two.

Does the local market help or hurt your odds?

Volusia and Flagler County are established, year-round markets with a mix of primary residents, second-home buyers, and steady relocation activity, not a boom-and-bust tourist economy. That kind of market is a genuine advantage if you pair it with the right brokerage. Adams, Cameron & Co. has operated here since 1963, so the brand recognition that helps a listing presentation or a cold introduction already exists before you make your first call. A strong market lowers the ceiling on how hard the first year has to be. It does not remove the requirement to work it.

What actually separates agents who make it

Not talent, and not luck. The agents who are still in the business three years later almost always had three things from day one: real training instead of a sink-or-swim orientation, a non-competing manager who was actually reachable when a deal got complicated, and marketing and CRM tools that didn’t come out of their own pocket while they were barely making an income. Adams, Cameron & Co. built its new-agent onboarding, including AC Social, FRED, and DeltaNet CRM, around exactly those three things, precisely because that gap is what causes most first-year agents to quit before they ever got a fair shot.

Which situation are you in?

The honest answer above is general. These are the specific situations people actually ask about most, each with its own honest answer.

Coming from a specific career:

  • Can teachers transition into real estate?
  • Can nurses and healthcare workers transition into real estate?
  • Can military veterans transition into real estate?
  • Can you become an agent with no sales experience?
  • Changing careers into real estate, the honest bottom line

Based on your life stage or circumstances:

  • Can stay-at-home parents start a real estate career?
  • Is real estate a good career for parents with young kids?
  • Can you become an agent after retirement?
  • Is there a best age to start a real estate career?
  • Is real estate a good fit if you just moved to Florida?

Worried about personal fit:

  • Is real estate a good career for introverts?
  • Is real estate a good fit if you hate cold calling?
  • Can you become an agent with bad credit?

None of these situations, on their own, are disqualifying. But want a real number instead of a list to read through? Take the honest self-assessment and rate yourself on the factors that actually predict a good first year.

The honest bottom line

Real estate is a good career if you can handle commission-only income for a slow first stretch, you’re genuinely comfortable with sales and self-direction, and you choose a brokerage that will actually train and support you rather than just activate your license and wish you luck. It is not a good career if you need a paycheck in week one, or if the idea of being your own boss sounds better than it actually feels once you’re living it. Decide honestly which one describes you before you enroll in a course.

This is educational, not financial or career advice. Talk through your specific situation with a broker before you commit to a course or a brokerage.

faq.q: Is real estate a good career choice?
faq.a: It can be, for the right person: someone comfortable with commission-only income, self-directed work, and a slower first year while a client pipeline builds. It's a poor fit for someone who needs a steady paycheck immediately or dislikes sales and rejection. The market itself can be a genuine advantage, but only once you're paired with a brokerage that trains and supports new agents.

faq.q: How long does it take to make money as a new real estate agent?
faq.a: Most new agents describe the first six to twelve months as the slowest, before referrals and repeat clients start carrying the business. Having savings or another income source to cover that stretch, and a brokerage that provides real training and leads, are the two biggest factors in getting through it.

faq.q: Do real estate agents get a salary?
faq.a: No. Real estate agents are independent contractors, not employees of their brokerage. There is no base salary or guaranteed hours; income comes entirely from commissions on closed transactions.

faq.q: What's the biggest reason new real estate agents quit?
faq.a: Running out of savings or patience during the slow first year, usually made worse by a brokerage that provided little training, no leads, and no accessible manager. The agents who make it past year one almost always had real onboarding and support from day one.

faq.q: How do I know if a real estate career is right for me?
faq.a: Be honest about two things: can you handle commission-only income with no guaranteed paycheck for several months, and do you genuinely like sales, prospecting, and being self-directed rather than managed. If both are true, the career can work well, especially with the right brokerage behind you.
